title: Lindsay King-Miller explores new angles to horror's "possession narrative"
excerpt: In the Colorado Book Award-winning "This Is My Body," the author offered a queer, agnostic take on the classic exorcism story.
content:
Lindsay King-Miller is the author of “The Z Word” and the Colorado Book Award winner “This Is My Body.” She is an instructor in the Graduate Program of Creative Writing at Western Colorado University. She lives in Denver with her partner and their two children.

SunLit: “This Is My Body” won this year’s Colorado Book Award for Mystery, Thriller and Horror. Which of those genres fits the narrative best, and how would you describe the story of your protagonist, Brigid, and her daughter, Dylan? 

Lindsay King-Miller: “This Is My Body” is a horror novel offering a queer, agnostic take on the classic exorcism story. Brigid, a gay single mom, believes her daughter’s strange behavior may be a sign of demonic possession. With nowhere else to turn and despite decades of estrangement, she seeks help from her Catholic priest uncle, but saving her daughter will be more complicated than “the power of Christ compels you.”

UNDERWRITTEN BY

Each week, The Colorado Sun and Colorado Humanities & Center For The Book feature an excerpt from a Colorado book and an interview with the author. Explore the SunLit archives at coloradosun.com/sunlit.

SunLit: The title “This Is My Body” carries many possible meanings. What was your thinking and how did you arrive at the title?

King-Miller: I brainstormed possible titles drawn from Bible verses and the Catholic mass. “This Is My Body” felt like the right fit, because it suggests the battle between a possessed person and the demon inhabiting their body. It also sounds like something an adolescent girl like Dylan might cry out in protest while her mother, her school, the Church, and countless other social and political forces battle for control of her body and her future.

SunLit: What makes possession such a compelling horror device, and how do you use it to explore the various themes in the novel? 

King-Miller: I’m very interested in possession narratives as someone who was raised Catholic and no longer believes. William Peter Blatty launched the whole subgenre with “The Exorcist,” and Blatty was a devout Catholic, so that influence still resonates through most exorcism narratives.

They tend to be about good versus evil struggling for control of the possessed person, who is often a young woman or girl. It’s not about what the girl wants but about whether someone else, an outside force, can save her, which makes sense in the context of a religion where you’re supposed to put yourself in God’s hands. I wanted to write a story where the possessed girl can speak back to those outside forces. She might not have a lot of power — adolescent girls usually don’t — but she can name what’s happening to her and say it’s not fair.

SunLit: What can a queer perspective reveal about the possession narrative that might be overlooked in a more traditional horror story?

King-Miller: Because most exorcism stories are rooted in Catholicism, they just don’t address queer perspectives. You can’t really say the Catholic God is the only authority and the only defense against evil, but also, queer people are valid. In order to write an exorcism story from a queer perspective I had to question the dogma that’s part of the genre’s DNA. I had to undermine the authority of the Church, which took the book to a place that I think is very different from most exorcism stories.

SunLit: You’ve mentioned that you had a childhood fascination with the famous Goosebumps series. How did those books influence you and can readers see that influence in your current work?

King-Miller: That’s a good question! I know when I first started writing stories, when I was about 7, I was basically writing Goosebumps knockoffs. I don’t think R.L. Stine’s influence really shows up in my writing today — it’s been about 30 years since I last read his work — but I love that he made horror fun and accessible for kids and gave us an on-ramp into the genre.

SunLit: Does horror offer unique possibilities as a genre for exploring subjects like religious trauma or even family conflict that’s evident in “This Is My Body”?

King-Miller: Absolutely. Horror has such a rich vocabulary of images and tropes, monsters and hauntings and extreme events, that I think can be so effective for expressing extreme emotions. There’s a level of intensity that we feel, but it’s hard to express in literal terms. Horror gives us a shape for those feelings, not just fear but the far reaches of desire, anger, guilt, or grief. I’ve said often that horror is the genre best equipped to handle grief.

SunLit: The book contains some disturbing moments, but it’s also a story about love, survival, and reclaiming yourself. What do you hope stays with readers? 

King-Miller: I wouldn’t mind if it’s those extreme moments, to be honest! When someone says “this gross scene you wrote haunted me for days,” I feel like I’ve done my job. But beyond that, I think for me the book is about trying to parent your children the best you can while knowing you’re not perfect and you’ll get it wrong sometimes.

It’s the most important work you’ll ever do and you’re going to make mistakes and hurt this little person who trusts and depends on you. I’m not offering any answers or solutions for that, but I hope maybe people can read it and feel that they’re not alone. That’s a lot of what draws me to horror: the honesty in it, the recognition of real experiences that are so difficult and so frightening, but at least we’re not alone.

SunLit: Tell us about your creative process. When, where and how do you write?

King-Miller: I’m a full-time parent to a high needs child, so I write whenever and wherever I can! Sometimes that’s at the library on weekends, but a lot of the time it’s on my phone while my kids are playing video games. I know there are some great organizing tools for writers these days, but I just work in Google Docs.

SunLit: You’ve written both fiction and nonfiction. What can readers look forward to in your next project?

King-Miller: I have an idea for another nonfiction book but it’s off in the future somewhere. I’ve been working on a historical horror novel set in Denver’s Cheesman Park, where the city’s first cemetery was once located, and I’m hoping to have more to share about that soon. I just started brainstorming a new novel with Rachel Feder, author of “The Turn” and “Taylor Swift By the Book.” I’m also working on putting together a manuscript for what I hope will be my first poetry collection.

A few more quick items

Currently on your nightstand for recreational reading: “The Gilda Stories” by Jewelle Gomez. I read horror year-round, but October feels like the right time for vampires.

First book you remember really making an impression on you as a kid: One of my earliest memories is my dad reading “The Hobbit” to me. I must have been 5 or 6. The riddle contest in the cave was so scary and fascinating.

Best writing advice you’ve ever received:  My high school writing teacher, Jana Clark, always used to say, “Keep your hand moving.” That meant: don’t edit as you go, don’t overthink, just keep writing. The best work comes when you write so fast your self-conscious, critical brain can’t keep up. I still follow this rule more than 20 years later.

Favorite fictional literary character: Like a character who’s a writer, or just a character from literature? The answer to the first — I could overthink this but I’m going to go with my first instinct, which is Bill Denbrough from Stephen King’s “It.” My favorite character from any book ever? That’s impossible! I’m going to say Gideon Nav from “Gideon the Ninth” by Tamsyn Muir, but please know I’ll be second-guessing this decision for weeks.

Literary guilty pleasure (title or genre): Feeling guilty about reading? Couldn’t be me. I might occasionally feel embarrassed about my enjoyment of fan fiction, but that’s different from guilt. As long as I’m reading work by human writers, I’m not hurting anyone!

Digital, print or audio – favorite medium to consume literature: All of the above! I’m usually reading at least one book in each format. My preference depends on genre to some extent: I like listening to nonfiction audiobooks, especially if they’re narrated by the writer. For poetry, I prefer print. I want to interpret the poems as I read them, not hear them in someone else’s voice. Horror is perfect in any format.

One book you’ve read multiple times: “Lone Women” by Victor LaValle

Other than writing utensils, one thing you must have within reach when you write: A drink or two, ideally one cold seltzer and one chai, hot or iced depending on the weather

Best antidote for writer’s block: Lower your standards and keep writing! Most of the time, writer’s block is another name for perfectionism. Be brave; write badly.

Most valuable beta reader: My partner Charlie and one close friend are the first to read anything I write. They’re loving and positive, of course, but they’ll also tell me if they think something isn’t working. And their encouragement buoys me up for whatever critique I have to deal with later in the writing process.

Type of Story: Q&A

An interview to provide a relevant perspective, edited for clarity and not fully fact-checked.
